keyVerseText: But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, (then saith he to the sick of the palsy,) Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house.
rootMeaning: The Greek word οἶκος (oîkos) carries the fundamental idea of a dwelling place or home, encompassing not only physical houses but also more expansive or figurative abodes such as temples or family units. Since its etymology is uncertain, the core meaning derived from its usage highlights a place of habitation and belonging, which extends beyond mere structure to include the concept of household and family community. This enriches the English gloss by emphasizing relational and spiritual dimensions implicit in the term.
usageInScripture: With 114 occurrences, οἶκος is predominantly translated as 'house' or 'the house,' reflecting its primary sense as a physical dwelling. However, it also appears in contexts referring to temples, public buildings, or figurative homes such as the body or the community of believers, demonstrating a versatile range. The consistency of translations like 'house,' 'houses,' and 'home' reveals its broad semantic field that embraces both literal and metaphorical spaces of habitation and belonging within Scripture.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding οἶκος as more than a mere building enriches our grasp of biblical teaching about God’s presence and the people of God. It signifies not only physical structures but also the spiritual household of faith, including the temple and the body of Christ. This word points to God’s desire to dwell among His people and for believers to live in unity as a family under His lordship. Recognizing οἶκος in its full biblical sense invites believers to see themselves as integral parts of God’s household, called to embody His presence and love in the world.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 9:6, Jesus commands the paralytic to 'Arise, take up thy bed, and go unto thine house,' using οἶκος to denote the patient's own dwelling place. This highlights the restoration not only of physical health but also of personal and social wholeness, enabling the man to return to his home and community. The word οἶκος here underscores the significance of home as a place of belonging and normal life, made possible through Christ’s authority to forgive sins and heal.
